title: Seeing Your Partner a Little Better
text:
Sandra Murray, John Holmes and Dale Griffin, working at the University of Waterloo in Canada, wondered whether happy couples see each other accurately or through a slightly rosy lens. They recruited both dating and married couples and asked each person to rate themselves, their partner and their ideal partner on a long list of qualities, such as kind, understanding, patient, critical or lazy.

This allowed a clever comparison. The researchers could see how each person viewed their partner, and how that partner viewed themselves. If a woman rated her husband as more patient and understanding than he rated himself, she was seeing him through a positive illusion.

That is what many people did. They tended to see their partners more generously than the partners saw themselves, and their image of their partner resembled their image of an ideal partner. These positive illusions went along with greater satisfaction. People were happier when they idealized their partners, and also when they were idealized by them.

In a related follow-up, the same team found that dating couples who idealized each other more were more likely to stay together and to become more satisfied over time, as if being seen at one's best helped people live up to it.
lesson: Look at the people you love a little more generously than strict accuracy requires. Being seen at your best can help you become it.
people: Sandra Murray, John Holmes, Dale Griffin
source: Murray, S. L., Holmes, J. G., and Griffin, D. W. (1996). The benefits of positive illusions: Idealization and the construction of satisfaction in close relationships. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 70(1), 79-98.
